tasks.title: University Admissions
tasks.subtitle: Build a predictor you can defend.
tasks.description: Learn from synthetic applicant records, validate your choices, and submit admission probabilities.
tasks.deliverable: One CSV with ID and Felvételi Eredmény for every validation and test row.
tasks.adaptation: Original public training data is split into training, validation, and final holdout. Scores are local practice ROC AUC, not the original leaderboard.
tasks.statement:
University Admissions

Use Notebook & files to make your own Colab copy. Export the ZIP when you finish, then follow Grading & notes on the task page. The grader returns validation and final practice results from public practice fixtures.

You work with synthetic applicant records from the Hungarian AI Olympiad's 2025 online qualifier. Predict the probability that each applicant is admitted.

Your first ten minutes

  1. Open Starter.ipynb and run the baseline from top to bottom.
  2. Inspect the labeled rows and the class balance.
  3. Write down what ROC AUC measures and why the output is a probability rather than a hard label.
  4. Export the generated predictions.csv and follow Grading & notes.

Supplied files

  • train.csv: labeled examples. The target is Felvételi Eredmény and the identifier is ID.
  • validation.csv: unlabeled rows used for feedback during an attempt.
  • test.csv: unlabeled rows used only for final evaluation after you finish.
  • counties.geojson: the original geographic companion file.
  • original_test.csv: the original competition's unlabeled test set, included for completeness. It is not part of pilot scoring.
  • Source_Reading.ipynb: the original source notebook as a reading copy, with outputs removed and punctuation normalized. Its original platform paths are not the pilot's paths.

The supplied training rows are 70% of the original public training data. Validation and final test each contain 15%, with a fixed stratified split. Their labels are reserved for evaluation. The free repository's practice fixtures are public and inspectable. Do not use external data or attempt to recover withheld answers from the source repository.

Work and improve

Make a development split inside train.csv before choosing features and models. The provided baseline uses only school prestige. Compare it with one carefully chosen improvement. Inspect errors and record the split and metric. Optional geographic features can use the county names and coordinates in the supplied GeoJSON.

Use Python, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, and the supplied companion data. All required packages are installed. No downloads are needed.

Submit

Export one UTF-8 CSV with exactly two columns: ID,Felvételi Eredmény. Include every ID from both validation.csv and test.csv exactly once. Every prediction must be finite and between 0 and 1. Row order does not matter.

The grader reports ROC AUC and log loss on both practice splits. Higher ROC AUC is better. In independent mode, score your ZIP after finishing the attempt.

Explain before moving on

Which feature change helped on your own development split? Could an identifier, duplicate, or county grouping create misleading validation? Can someone else recreate the CSV from your saved notebook?

Provenance and pilot changes

Source: Hungarian AI Olympiad, 2025 summer online qualifier. English translation credited to Tamás Takács, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. This educational adaptation preserves source credit. The local split and submission arrangement differ from the original Kaggle event. These are practice results, not official competition scores.

tasks.title: Debugging U-Net
tasks.subtitle: Make the shapes and the metric agree.
tasks.description: Repair the supplied network's center crop and implement mean intersection over union.
tasks.deliverable: One Python file exporting BrokenUNet and calculate_miou.
tasks.adaptation: The pilot uses automated checks for the two coding parts. The supplied notebook's missing-class example is corrected to 0.375. The architecture produces 110 by 110 outputs for 256 by 256 inputs.
tasks.statement:
Debugging U-Net

Use Notebook & files to make your own Colab copy. Export the ZIP when you finish, then follow Grading & notes on the task page. The grader returns validation and final practice results from public practice fixtures.

The supplied network has valid convolutions, so its feature maps shrink. Its skip connection does not fit the decoder tensor. Repair the center crop and implement a trustworthy segmentation metric.

Your first ten minutes

  1. Open submission.py beside Starter.ipynb in JupyterLab.
  2. Run the notebook's initial check and read the failure.
  3. Trace height and width through the supplied layers on paper.
  4. Edit the two unfinished methods in submission.py, save it, and rerun the notebook checks.

Part 1: architecture, 10 points

Keep the supplied architecture, convolution padding, layer names, and forward order. Implement BrokenUNet.center_crop(layer, target_shape) and use it to align the encoder feature map before concatenation. For an odd difference, put the extra discarded pixel on the bottom or right.

The grader checks cropping on varied tensor shapes and values, layer structure, output dimensions, and a real forward pass. A 256 by 256 input produces a 110 by 110 output with this exact architecture. Do not resize the final output to 256 by 256.

Part 2: metric, 10 points

Implement calculate_miou(pred_mask, true_mask, num_classes=2). Inputs are integer class maps of shape B by H by W. For each class, divide intersection by union. Average the values of classes with a nonzero union. Skip a class only when it appears in neither prediction nor truth. Return 0.0 for an empty input.

You may loop over classes. Do not loop over individual pixels or batches. Use only torch, torch.nn, torch.nn.functional, and NumPy. Metric wrappers and architecture substitutions are not permitted.

Important source correction

The original notebook's additional missing-class self-check is inconsistent with its own formula. For prediction [[0,0],[0,1]] and truth [[0,0],[0,0]], class 0 has IoU 3/4 and class 1 has IoU 0/1. The correct mean is 0.375, not 0.75. A false positive still contributes to the union. The pilot's checks follow the formula.

The original output-size examples are illustrative and do not match this exact architecture. The pilot uses the measured output size of 110 by 110.

Submit

Package submission.py, exporting BrokenUNet and calculate_miou. Do not include notebook display or training code in that file. The starter already separates the editable submission from the notebook checks. The evaluator runs code in an isolated process with a 90-second wall-clock limit. No GPU or model training is needed.

Validation feedback lists passed and failed checks. The final practice evaluation uses a separate set of generated tensors. Scores are automated pilot checks out of 20, not an official exam mark.

Explain before moving on

Why does cropping lose border information? How does an always-background prediction behave under pixel accuracy versus mean IoU? Which test caught a mistake your first example missed?

Provenance

Source: Singapore NOAI 2026 final assessment, programming task 2, published by AISGNUSNOAI. The supplied task and architecture are retained. Corrections and the pilot's automated evaluation are identified above. Source_Reading.ipynb preserves the source content for comparison, with outputs removed and punctuation normalized.

tasks.title: Catacomb Adventure
tasks.subtitle: Turn experience into a way out.
tasks.description: Explore the authentic environment, find a safe route, and learn Monte Carlo and SARSA action values.
tasks.deliverable: One JSON file with actions, mc_q, and sarsa_q. Each Q table has shape 56 by 4.
tasks.adaptation: Automated pilot scoring covers the fixed 2025 map, a route, and two learned tables. The original plots, zombie experiments, and written explanations remain available for peer review and are not automatically graded.
tasks.statement:
Catacomb Adventure

Use Notebook & files to make your own Colab copy. Export the ZIP when you finish, then follow Grading & notes on the task page. The grader returns validation and final practice results from public practice fixtures.

Help the heroine escape the authentic CreepyCatacombs-v0 environment. Learn how a route, a reward, and an action-value table describe different parts of the same decision problem.

Your first ten minutes

  1. Open Starter.ipynb and reset the environment with seed 2025.
  2. Display the map and locate the entrance, exit, walls, and pits.
  3. Take one action and inspect observation, reward, termination, and truncation.
  4. Run the starter export and grade the ZIP once to establish a measured starting point.

The environment

The pinned package is creepy-catacombs-s1==0.1.4, the version used by the original task. It has 56 discrete states on an 8 by 7 map and four actions: 0 up, 1 right, 2 down, 3 left. Reset with seed 2025 for the pilot. Do not confuse an episode ending naturally with its time limit being reached.

The automated pilot uses the original no-zombie map. The full source notebook also includes changing layouts, zombies, plots, Monte Carlo control, SARSA, and visualizations. Those remain useful extensions for peer review.

Version 0.1.4 terminates when entering the goal but leaves agent_pos on the preceding square and gives the ordinary -1 step reward. Identify success from termination and the attempted destination, not a positive reward or the final reported position. The pilot also requires a safe route without wall, pit, or out-of-bounds steps. Use a separate np.random.default_rng for exploration because the environment reset also resets NumPy's global random seed.

Build three results

  1. Find a safe action sequence from entrance to exit on the fixed map.
  2. Implement Monte Carlo control and export its learned Q table.
  3. Implement SARSA and export its learned Q table.

Train on the supplied fixed environment. Exploration is allowed during training. During evaluation, the table chooses a greedy action. Ties are broken with a documented evaluation seed. Use complete episode returns for Monte Carlo and the next chosen action for SARSA. Keep terminated and truncated separate in your loop.

Submit

Export a JSON object with three keys: - actions: at most 500 integer actions from 0 through 3. - mc_q: 56 rows of 4 finite action values from your Monte Carlo run. - sarsa_q: 56 rows of 4 finite action values from your SARSA run.

The notebook export cell packages the JSON for evaluation. Save the notebook and reward curves in your own workspace for review.

Pilot scoring

The route contributes 20 points, Monte Carlo contributes 40, and SARSA contributes 40. A failed escape receives 0 for that part. A successful escape receives half the part's points plus the other half multiplied by shortest safe route length divided by steps taken. A shortest successful route earns full credit. Value tables are evaluated over five rollouts with fixed, published tie-breaking seeds for validation. Final evaluation uses five different tie-breaking seeds.

This is a fixed-map demonstration. It does not measure generalization to unseen maps. Plots, whether a table was actually learned, the zombie experiments, and the original written explanations require notebook review. The pilot's automated score is not the original 100-plus-15-point rubric.

Explain before moving on

Show one state whose action values changed during learning. Explain one difference between Monte Carlo and SARSA. Show that a successful policy can be reloaded without retraining. Then try the optional zombie experiment in the source notebook.

Provenance

Source: Hungarian AI Olympiad, 2025 summer national final. English translation credited to Tamás Takács, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The pilot adds a JSON submission format and the clearly described automatic scoring above. The original question sequence is supplied in Source_Reading.ipynb as a reading copy.

tasks.title: Basketball Shooting
tasks.subtitle: Can two coordinates predict a shot?
tasks.description: Can two coordinates predict a shot?
tasks.source_name: China NOAI 2024 task, republished in the APOAI 2025 mock
tasks.deliverable: One ZIP containing submission_model.py and submission_dic.pth.
tasks.adaptation: Practice uses a fixed 70/15/15 split of the public data. Original hidden competition data is unavailable. Scores measure this practice split.
tasks.statement:
Basketball Shooting

Use Notebook & files to make your own Colab copy. Export the ZIP when you finish, then follow Grading & notes on the task page. The grader returns validation and final practice results from public practice fixtures.

Use the location of a basketball shot to predict whether it goes in. Start by asking whether shots near the basket have a different success rate. A small model and a sound validation split matter more than a large network here.

Your first ten minutes

  1. Open Starter.ipynb. It loads train.csv and shows the first rows.
  2. Plot loc_x against loc_y, colouring points by shot_made_flag.
  3. Run the deliberately untrained starter once to check packaging and submission.
  4. Make a development split inside train.csv before choosing a training method.

Data and model rules

The supplied train.csv contains 17,500 labeled shots, 70% of the 25,000 rows in the public mirror. Validation and final test each use 3,750 different rows. Their labels are reserved for evaluation. The free repository's practice fixtures are public and inspectable. These are practice partitions, not the original hidden competition test.

Use only loc_x and loc_y as model inputs, in that order. Predict shot_made_flag, where 1 means a made shot. The other columns are supplied for context and cannot be inputs. Do not fetch the original public labels for the withheld rows.

Implement PyTorch class MyModel with a no-argument constructor. Use one to three nn.Linear layers, each with at most eight output neurons. Other permitted leaf modules are nn.ReLU, nn.Sigmoid, nn.Tanh, nn.ELU, nn.LeakyReLU, and nn.PReLU. Do not use nn.Sequential. Return one raw logit per row, shape N or N by 1. The evaluator applies sigmoid and thresholds at 0.5. Fit preprocessing on your training rows only and include it in the exported model. Inputs at evaluation are the original CSV coordinates.

Submit and improve

Save submission.zip with exactly submission_model.py and submission_dic.pth at its root. The Python file defines MyModel and imports. The weights file is a torch state_dict. Do not include training code that executes when imported. Maximum ZIP size is 8 MB. The notebook includes a packaging cell.

Validation feedback reports accuracy and majority-class accuracy. The final practice evaluation uses the other 3,750 rows. Accuracy is the primary score. Save the split, seed, loss, and one explanation of your errors in the notebook.

Source and changes

This is China NOAI 2024 task 1, republished as APOAI 2025 mock task 1. The linked original statement describes 20,000 training rows, while the public mirror contains 25,000. This room uses the mirror and its own disclosed partitions. The architecture and model ZIP contract are retained. Read Source_Statement.md for a punctuation-normalized source reading copy.

tasks.title: Real or Fake Images
tasks.subtitle: Learn visual evidence, then test it.
tasks.description: Learn visual evidence, then test it.
tasks.source_name: China NOAI 2024 task, republished in the APOAI 2025 mock
tasks.deliverable: One ZIP containing submission_model.py and submission_dic.pth.
tasks.adaptation: Practice uses a fixed 70/15/15 split of the public data. Original hidden competition data is unavailable. Image scoring uses ordinary accuracy, without the historical doubling bug.
tasks.statement:
Real or Fake Images

Use Notebook & files to make your own Colab copy. Export the ZIP when you finish, then follow Grading & notes on the task page. The grader returns validation and final practice results from public practice fixtures.

Distinguish real CIFAR images from generated images. Both classes are small RGB images of the same dimensions. Look for repeatable visual evidence rather than memorizing filenames.

Your first ten minutes

  1. Open Starter.ipynb and extract images_train.zip.
  2. Display several images from each class, using train.csv as the label map.
  3. Run the untrained starter and export its model ZIP to check the submission path.
  4. Make a stratified development split before training or changing the network.

Data and preprocessing

The pack contains 7,000 labeled 32 by 32 RGB training images. Real is 0 and generated is 1. The evaluator reserves 1,500 images for validation and 1,500 different images for final testing from the same public 10,000-image archive. This is a fixed stratified 70/15/15 practice split. Original hidden competition images are unavailable.

Use float32 input tensors in N by 3 by 32 by 32 order, normalized with pixel / 127.5 - 1. Use the same normalization in training and evaluation. The evaluator supplies these normalized tensors directly.

Model rules

Implement PyTorch class MyModel with a no-argument constructor. Include at least two nn.Conv2d and two nn.MaxPool2d modules, used in the forward pass. Use at most two nn.Linear modules. Permitted activation modules are nn.ReLU, nn.Sigmoid, nn.Tanh, nn.ELU, nn.LeakyReLU, and nn.PReLU. Do not use nn.Sequential. Other leaf modules are not accepted. Tensor operations such as reshape and flatten are allowed.

Return one probability per image, shape N or N by 1, between 0 and 1. The evaluator thresholds at 0.5. This differs from Basketball Shooting's raw-logit contract. A final sigmoid is a straightforward way to satisfy it.

Submit and scoring

Save submission.zip with exactly submission_model.py and submission_dic.pth at its root. The Python file defines MyModel and imports. Save a torch state_dict as the weights file. Keep training outside the submitted class file. Maximum ZIP size is 8 MB.

Feedback reports accuracy, counted convolutional and linear layers, and the practice composite score:

simplicity = 1 / (number_of_linear_layers + number_of_convolutional_layers + 1)
score = 0.75 * (accuracy + simplicity)

The original statement mentions a historical bug that doubled accuracy. This practice evaluator uses ordinary accuracy. Its score therefore cannot be compared numerically with that historical leaderboard. The final practice evaluation uses different held-out images.

Source and review

This is China NOAI 2024 task 2, republished as APOAI 2025 mock task 2. Source_Statement.md contains a reading copy. The public archive supplies 5,000 real and 5,000 generated images. Do not recover withheld labels from the original archive during an independent attempt. Explain one false positive, one false negative, and whether an improvement survived your own development split.

tasks.title: Pendulum Motion
tasks.subtitle: Recover the physics behind missing observations.
tasks.description: Recover the physics behind missing observations.
tasks.source_name: China NOAI 2024 task, republished in the APOAI 2025 mock
tasks.deliverable: One Python file exporting solve(frame), returning the five named parameters.
tasks.adaptation: Practice uses synthetic recordings from the stated equation with known answers. Submit solve(frame) instead of the original complete notebook. Original hidden A and B recordings are unavailable.
tasks.statement:
Pendulum Motion

Use Notebook & files to make your own Colab copy. Export the ZIP when you finish, then follow Grading & notes on the task page. The grader returns validation and final practice results from public practice fixtures.

A sensor records a damped pendulum, loses a continuous interval, then resumes recording. During that gap, a constant downward force is switched on. Recover the physical parameters and predict the next zero crossing after the last observation.

Your first ten minutes

  1. Open Starter.ipynb and plot t against theta from pendulum_train.csv.
  2. Inspect consecutive time differences and locate the missing interval.
  3. Read the equation below and identify what changes when the force begins.
  4. Open submission.py. Its solve(frame) function initially returns deliberately poor default values. Run it once and make a first submission to check the path.

Given physics

Mass is 1 and gravity is 9.8. Initial angular velocity is zero. Angles are radians and time is seconds.

theta''(t) = -alpha * theta'(t) - beta * sin(theta(t))
alpha = miu
beta_before = 9.8 / l
beta_after = (9.8 + F) / l

The force starts once during the missing interval and stays on. Use PyTorch for the regression step. NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and math are also available. Do not estimate a derivative by connecting observations across the missing interval. Your approach must adapt to a new recording, not return constants fitted to the supplied one.

Data and practice evaluation

pendulum_train.csv is the original public 734-row recording, with columns t and theta. Its hidden true parameters are not publicly supplied, so the room does not invent an official score for it.

Validation uses two synthetic recordings from the stated equation, with different parameters. Final testing uses two further recordings. All have initial velocity zero, one missing interval longer than one second, and a force switch inside that gap. Practice lengths are 3 to 6, resistance 0.2 to 0.6, forces 20 to 45, initial angles 0.6 to 1.1, and observations from 0 to 15 seconds. These are disclosed practice ranges, not inferred limits of the original contest.

Submission contract

Package submission.py defining solve(frame). frame is a pandas DataFrame with t and theta only. Return exactly a dictionary with finite numeric values for l, miu, F, t_nextzerotheta, and t_Fput. The function is called independently on each recording. t_nextzerotheta must be the first zero crossing strictly after the final observation. Maximum source size is 2 MB. Validation evaluation has a 90-second total time limit.

This callable replaces the original full submission notebook so the room can rerun a method on withheld recordings. Keep derivations, plots, and training steps in Starter.ipynb for review. The linked original statement describes submission_train.csv, submissionA.csv, and submissionB.csv. Those files are not the room's submission contract.

Scoring

For absolute errors e_l, e_miu, e_F, e_next, and e_switch:

score = (exp(-10*e_l) + exp(-10*e_miu) + 2*exp(-e_F)
         + 2*exp(-10*e_next) + 2*exp(-10*e_switch)) / 8

The room averages this score across recordings. One is perfect and larger is better. Feedback includes each parameter's mean absolute error. The grader also evaluates separate final practice recordings. This uses the source metric on practice fixtures, not official hidden A or B data.

Source and review

China NOAI 2024 task 4, republished as APOAI 2025 mock task 4. Source_Statement.md includes the problem and score, with the solved appendix omitted. Explain how you handle the gap, why a force change modifies the frequency, and how you check the inferred trajectory against the observed one.
